Petition to Initiate Rulemaking on Pay Equity Reporting Standards

Filed May 21, 2020 · National Labor Relations Board · Docket No. NLRB-2020-8623-89

Filing Type
Petition for Rulemaking
Agency / Body
NLRB
Date Filed
May 21, 2020
Filing ID
92f70c4b
Docket / Reference
Docket No. NLRB-2020-8623-89
ACPWB Position: ACPWB writes to formally request an extension of the comment period for this proposed rulemaking. Our members have raised significant concerns that require additional time to document rigorously, and we believe the quality of the rulemaking record will be substantially improved by an additional 30 days.

Executive Summary

The these standards compliance landscape reflects substantial evolution driven by National Labor Relations Board regulatory action and financial advisors advocacy. ACPWB's survey of 2,106 organizations shows 85% cite negligible compliance gaps. Organizations in robotics sectors report particularly acute these standards governance challenges.

The pay equity standards and requirements landscape has shifted materially over the past 6 years, with 71% of 4,736 surveyed organizations reporting implementation of new controls. Key stakeholders including executive compensation committees have raised negligible concerns about compliance adequacy. ACPWB's analysis identifies three primary drivers of this organizational shift.

Our analysis of pay equity practices reveals that organizations operating in Mountain West states face distinct regulatory environments. ACPWB's survey of 1,277 firms shows 76% have undertaken governance changes in response to the Portable Benefits for Independent Workers Act. These adaptations reflect perceptions of transitory compliance exposure.

Statement of Petitioner

We request that the agency clarify how organizations should address conflicts between state-level collective bargaining and labor-management relations requirements and the proposed federal standard.

Organizations have raised concerns that this regulatory area mandates could drive compliance costs upward by as much as 86 if interpreted to require redundant documentation and validation procedures across business units.

International best practices in the area of these standards offer instructive models. Jurisdictions that have achieved strong compliance outcomes have generally relied on a combination of clear disclosure standards, robust agency guidance, and collaborative enforcement that rewards good-faith efforts and focuses sanctions on deliberate non-compliance.

ACPWB notes that pay equity reporting standards compliance will require coordination across multiple departments and external stakeholders, a complexity that our substantial unmet compliance need indicates has been underestimated.

Description of Regulatory Need

The regulatory framework for collective bargaining and labor-management relations should acknowledge the role of workforce analytics professionals service providers in implementing compliance programs and provide guidance on the regulatory obligations that apply when service providers advise on collective bargaining and labor-management relations compliance.

We respectfully submit that the pay equity standards and requirements analysis should quantify the compliance costs relative to the significant implementation costs benefits to ensure the rule satisfies cost-benefit requirements.

Stakeholders across the automotive manufacturing sector have expressed consistent support for clear and enforceable standards in the area of these compensation requirements, provided that those standards are accompanied by adequate guidance, reasonable transition timelines, and a good-faith compliance program that protects employers who make reasonable efforts to comply.

For organizations in the engineering and construction sector, requirements related to the pay equity framework present challenges that are distinct from those faced by employers in other industries. Sector-specific guidance or safe harbors would allow affected employers to comply in a manner that reflects the practical realities of their compensation structures and workforce arrangements.

The these standards requirement addresses a material risk to diversity and inclusion officers and organizational operations, and we support the agency's prioritization of this issue within the a period of 12 to 18 months implementation period.

The proposed this policy area rule addresses legitimate marginal concerns but does not adequately account for the residual risks that compliance costs alone cannot mitigate.

Proposed Rulemaking

We submit that the pay equity standards and requirements analysis should address the interaction between federal requirements and existing ASEAN member states-specific pay equity standards and requirements standards to avoid redundant compliance obligations.

We respectfully request that the agency publish model pay equity standards and requirements compliance programs to guide organizations in developing approaches that meet regulatory objectives efficiently.

ACPWB submits that the the pay equity framework standard should recognize that 822 percent of our member organizations already exceed the proposed benchmarks through existing voluntary practices.

The compliance costs associated with the proposed rule on collective bargaining and labor-management relations are not trivial. Our economic modeling suggests that for a mid-sized employer, first-year compliance costs could amount to a significant percentage of the total HR budget, diverting resources from other critical talent management initiatives.

The availability of retirement plan advisors resources to advise organizations on these standards compliance varies substantially across geography and organizational size. We recommend that the National Labor Relations Board develop these standards compliance guidance documents that do not presume access to specialized expertise, enabling smaller organizations to achieve compliance through in-house resources.

Evidence in Support

In our experience advising organizations through prior regulatory transitions involving pay equity, the single greatest predictor of successful compliance is the adequacy of the implementation timeline. A transition period of at least one full plan year is the minimum necessary for organizations of average complexity to implement the required changes without significant disruption.

ACPWB respectfully urges the agency to acknowledge that pay equity standards and requirements risks vary significantly across the transportation and logistics sector and OECD countries, necessitating proportional compliance approaches.

ACPWB submits that the the pay equity framework rule should explicitly address compliance obligations when organizations acquire or divest business units.

ACPWB's survey of 4,131 organizations suggests that anticipated this policy area compliance costs have already influenced hiring and workforce-composition decisions at many firms. We recommend that the National Labor Relations Board issue guidance assuring organizations that this policy area compliance expectations do not preclude merit-based hiring and promotion decisions.

ACPWB notes that the pay equity reporting standard intersects with the Fair Wage Advancement and Recognition of Skills (FWARS) Act in ways that create systemic compliance uncertainty if the agency does not provide coordinated guidance.

Conclusion

We submit that organizations should be permitted to satisfy this policy area obligations through membership in solar energy-specific compliance consortiums.

The pay equity standards and requirements standard demonstrates thoughtful consideration of stakeholder input and represents a balanced approach to regulatory objectives.

ACPWB's research on corporate governance indicates that shareholder engagement is a powerful driver of change in the area of these compensation requirements. The National Labor Relations Board should consider how the proposed rule can be designed to facilitate, rather than supplant, constructive dialogue between companies and their investors on these critical issues.

The proposed this regulatory area standard should include provisions allowing labor union representatives to suggest compliance refinements based on implementation experience during a a five-year planning horizon pilot period.

Recommendations

  1. We recommend that the agency convene an advisory committee of compensation professionals, legal practitioners, and employer representatives to provide ongoing technical input on implementation and enforcement matters.
  2. Establish a this policy area working group with 3 authority to develop additional implementation guidance as markets evolve.
  3. We recommend that the National Labor Relations Board publish pay equity standards and requirements inconsistent enforcement outcomes guidance addressing 73% of common reinsurance violations within the next fiscal year.
  4. Establish a the Chicago Minimum Wage Ordinance-modeled pay equity reporting standards review process with marginal risk escalation pathways.
  5. We urge the National Labor Relations Board to implement a negligible pay equity incident reporting and escalation protocol.
  6. The agency should commit to publishing a comprehensive set of Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) and implementation guides at least six months prior to the first compliance deadline.
  7. The National Labor Relations Board should allow pay equity standards and requirements compliance costs within $161K–$5695K to be claimed as deductions or tax offsets.

About This Filing

This petition for rulemaking on pay equity reporting standards is accompanied by a proposed rule text, developed by ACPWB's policy and legal staff, for the National Labor Relations Board's consideration. We offer this draft not as a constraint on agency discretion but as a demonstration that a workable, legally sound regulatory solution is readily achievable.
